prompt: Under which licence is OpenTofu published?
hint: Its licence file was shown in the lesson.

choices.text: Business Source License 1.1
choices.why: That is Terraform's licence from version 1.6.0 on.

choices.text: Apache 2.0
choices.why: That is the CDK's and Pulumi's licence.

choices.text: Mozilla Public License 2.0
choices.why: Yes: the licence Terraform had before August 2023, kept by the fork.

choices.text: A licence of its own written by the Linux Foundation
choices.why: The Linux Foundation hosts the project; the licence is the MPL the code already had.

prompt: The shop runs Terraform 1.16 on its own AWS account and sells nothing built on it. What does the BSL's additional use grant mean for the shop?
hint: Who does the licence exclude?

choices.text: It may keep running it in production, as it does now
choices.why: Right. The exclusion is offering Terraform to others in a product that competes with IBM's paid versions.

choices.text: It has to move to OpenTofu before the change date
choices.why: The change date turns a version into MPL; it imposes no deadline on users.

choices.text: It must buy a commercial licence from IBM
choices.why: Production use is granted; nothing in the terms charges an internal user.

choices.text: It may only use versions before 1.6.0
choices.why: Versions from 1.6.0 on are under the BSL, which still allows this use.

prompt: Why does OpenTofu's licence file still begin with HashiCorp's copyright?
hint: Where did the fork's code come from?

choices.text: HashiCorp co-maintains OpenTofu with the Linux Foundation
choices.why: HashiCorp does not maintain it; the fork exists because of HashiCorp's licence change.

choices.text: Most of its code was written by HashiCorp
choices.why: Yes: it is Terraform's code from before the change, and copyright stays with whoever wrote it.

choices.text: The BSL requires it in every derived work
choices.why: OpenTofu is not under the BSL; it forked from code published under the MPL.

choices.text: It is a leftover the project has not cleaned up
choices.why: A copyright notice records authorship; removing it would be wrong, not tidy.

prompt: Ana moves lesson 2's configuration to `tofu`. Which of these carry over unchanged? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section listed what does not differ.

choices.text: The HCL of `main.tf`
choices.why: Yes; the four resources were applied by `tofu` as written.

choices.text: The plan symbols and the state commands
choices.why: Yes; the commands are the same under another name.

choices.text: The `encryption` block from lesson 12, in Terraform
choices.why: Terraform refused that block; it exists only in OpenTofu.

choices.text: The version numbers of the two programs
choices.why: Terraform 1.16.4 and OpenTofu 1.13.1: they are numbered separately now.

choices.text: The `required_version = ">= 1.10"` check
choices.why: Yes; OpenTofu checks it against its own version, 1.13.1, and it passes.

prompt: In `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws`, which part is the provider's type?
hint: Three parts, read left to right.

choices.text: `registry.terraform.io`
choices.why: That is the registry's hostname.

choices.text: `hashicorp`
choices.why: That is the namespace.

choices.text: `aws`
choices.why: Yes: hostname, namespace, type.

choices.text: `hashicorp/aws` as a whole
choices.why: That is the short form: namespace and type, without the hostname.

prompt: On the machine these lessons were recorded on, whose providers came from a mirror, `tofu init` failed on `source = "hashicorp/aws"` and `terraform init` succeeded on the same file. Why?
hint: What did `tofu providers` print?

choices.text: OpenTofu cannot run the AWS provider HashiCorp publishes
choices.why: It ran exactly that provider once the address was written in full.

choices.text: The short form names another registry in OpenTofu
choices.why: Right: `registry.opentofu.org`, and that mirror was filed only under `registry.terraform.io`.

choices.text: The lock file had been written by Terraform first
choices.why: There was no lock file yet; `tofu init` was the first command in that directory.

choices.text: OpenTofu ignores the CLI configuration that points at the mirror
choices.why: It read it: the error lists the mirror's directory as the place it searched.

prompt: A local directory of provider packages, laid out by address and used instead of a registry, is called a filesystem ___.
hint: The recording machine's CLI configuration has a block of that name.

prompt: On her own laptop, with internet access and only `tofu` installed, how should Ana write the AWS provider's source?
hint: The full address was a property of something.

choices.text: `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws`, as in this lesson
choices.why: That was for the recording machine's mirror; OpenTofu does not need it.

choices.text: `opentofu/aws`, the fork's own provider
choices.why: The OpenTofu registry lists the same `hashicorp/aws`.

choices.text: `hashicorp/aws`
choices.why: Yes: OpenTofu completes it with its own registry, which lists the provider under that name.

choices.text: A path to the provider binary on disk
choices.why: `source` takes an address, never a file path.

prompt: After `tofu apply`, Terraform planned in the same directory and reported `No changes`. What made that possible?
hint: Look at what the state said, and at what the configuration used.

choices.text: Terraform converted the OpenTofu state on `terraform init`
choices.why: Nothing was converted; `init` only reused the provider from the lock file.

choices.text: The same format, and nothing only one of them knows
choices.why: Right: state `version` 4, the same provider address, and no feature like lesson 12's encryption.

choices.text: The `terraform_version` field said a version Terraform accepts
choices.why: It held OpenTofu's 1.13.1; the format version is what matters.

choices.text: Both programs share one registry
choices.why: Their default registries differ; that was the previous failure.

prompt: Where does CloudFormation keep the link between `ShopVpc` and the real VPC's id?
hint: There is no file.

choices.text: In a `terraform.tfstate` it writes beside the template
choices.why: That is Terraform's state; CloudFormation writes no file.

choices.text: In the stack, inside AWS
choices.why: Yes: `describe-stack-resources` lists logical and physical ids.

choices.text: In the VPC's Name tag
choices.why: A tag can be changed by anybody; the stack records the id.

choices.text: In the change set, until it expires
choices.why: A change set is the proposed changes; the stack holds the result.

prompt: Put Ana's CloudFormation steps in the order the lesson ran them.
hint: Review comes before anything is made.
items: Create a change set of type CREATE
Describe the change set and read the three `Add` lines
Delete the stack, which deletes the network
trap: Executing before describing skips the review the change set exists for.

prompt: A resource fails halfway through creating a new stack. What does CloudFormation do, compared with Terraform's partial apply in lesson 9?
hint: One keeps what succeeded; the other does not.

choices.text: It keeps what succeeded and retries the rest on the next deploy
choices.why: That is Terraform's behaviour.

choices.text: It rolls back, removing what it had already created for the stack
choices.why: Yes: it removes what it had created for that stack.

choices.text: It leaves the stack open for a manual fix
choices.why: By default it rolls back rather than waiting for a person.

choices.text: It writes the error into the template
choices.why: The template is your file; the stack's events record the failure.

prompt: Why does this lesson show a change set only for a stack being created, and not for an update?
hint: What is the lab's CloudFormation?

choices.text: CloudFormation has no change sets for existing stacks
choices.why: It does; on a real account they mark `Modify` and `Remove` and say whether a replacement is needed.

choices.text: An update has to go through `aws cloudformation deploy`
choices.why: `deploy` creates a change set itself; the command is not the obstacle.

choices.text: The lab's moto gets that answer wrong
choices.why: Right: it lists every resource as `Add`, so a capture would teach something false.

choices.text: Updates are what drift detection is for
choices.why: Drift detection compares resources with the template; it does not apply changes.

prompt: What does `cdk synth` produce?
hint: It ran offline.

choices.text: A Terraform plan for the AWS provider
choices.why: The CDK has nothing to do with Terraform; it writes CloudFormation.

choices.text: The resources themselves, created in AWS
choices.why: Synthesis asked AWS nothing; deploying is a later step.

choices.text: A CloudFormation template, written by running the program
choices.why: Yes; CloudFormation does the rest when it is deployed.

choices.text: A compiled binary of the app
choices.why: The program runs and its output is a template; nothing is compiled for AWS.

prompt: How many NAT gateways did the `ec2.Vpc` construct add with only a range and `maxAzs: 2`?
hint: Count them in the first resource count.

prompt: What did the second version of `app.js` change, and why did it matter?
hint: Compare the two counts.

choices.text: It switched to `CfnVPC` so the CDK would add nothing on its own
choices.why: It still uses `ec2.Vpc`; it stated the subnets and the NAT count instead of accepting the defaults.

choices.text: It set `natGateways: 0` and public `/24`s
choices.why: Yes: 24 resources became 12, with no NAT gateway billed by the hour.

choices.text: It added a region, so synthesis could reach AWS
choices.why: No region was added, and synthesis stays offline.

choices.text: It tagged the stack so the NAT gateways could be found
choices.why: The tag was added too, but the NAT gateways were removed, not found.

prompt: A colleague says the CDK means the shop no longer needs to worry about a state file. Is that right, and why?
hint: Who deploys what the CDK writes?

choices.text: No: `cdk.out` is the state and has to be committed
choices.why: `cdk.out` is build output the next synth rewrites; it is not committed.

choices.text: No: the bootstrap stack stores a state file in its bucket
choices.why: The bootstrap bucket holds files an app uploads, not a state.

choices.text: Yes: the state is the CloudFormation stack
choices.why: Right; the CDK only writes the template, and the stack keeps the record inside AWS.

choices.text: Yes: the CDK reads the real resources again on every deploy instead
choices.why: It does not need to; CloudFormation already keeps the record in the stack.

prompt: What does Pulumi do with the resources a program declares?
hint: It is not the CDK's answer.

choices.text: Writes them into a CloudFormation template
choices.why: That is the CDK; Pulumi produces no template for another service.

choices.text: Its engine compares them with its state and calls the API
choices.why: Yes, through a provider: Terraform's model with another language in front.

choices.text: Creates each one the moment `new` runs
choices.why: `new` registers the resource; the engine decides and creates later.

choices.text: Converts the program into HCL for Terraform
choices.why: Its providers are bridged from Terraform's, but no HCL is produced.

prompt: In the Pulumi program, `vpc.id` is an `Output`, not a string. What is the closest thing in a Terraform plan?
hint: A value nobody knows yet.

choices.text: `(known after apply)`
choices.why: Yes: a value that exists only once the VPC has been made.

choices.text: `(sensitive value)`
choices.why: That hides a known value; an `Output` is not known yet.

choices.text: A `variable` block with no default
choices.why: A variable is an input somebody supplies; the id comes from AWS.

choices.text: The `# forces replacement` comment
choices.why: That marks an argument whose change replaces a resource.

prompt: Where can a Pulumi stack's state be kept? Choose all that apply.
hint: The choice is made at `pulumi login`.

choices.text: Pulumi Cloud, the hosted service
choices.why: Yes, and it is the default.

choices.text: An S3 bucket
choices.why: Yes: `pulumi login s3://...`.

choices.text: A CloudFormation stack
choices.why: That is where the CDK's result lives; Pulumi keeps its own state.

choices.text: A local directory
choices.why: Yes: `pulumi login --local`.

choices.text: Inside `index.js`
choices.why: The program is the description; it never holds what was made.

prompt: Match each tool to where its state lives.
hint: One answer is a part of a template, not a place for state.

pairs.right: A file, in a backend you choose
Pulumi Cloud, a bucket or a directory

prompt: The shop also manages its DNS at a provider outside AWS and its GitHub organisation. Which tools in this lesson can hold all of it in one description?
hint: Which ones reach anything with a provider?

choices.text: CloudFormation and the CDK
choices.why: Both describe AWS only.

choices.text: Terraform, OpenTofu and Pulumi
choices.why: Yes: each reaches whatever has a provider.

choices.text: The CDK alone, because it is a general-purpose language
choices.why: The language does not widen what CloudFormation can create.

choices.text: Only Terraform, because the others were forked from it
choices.why: Only OpenTofu is a fork, and Pulumi has providers of its own.

prompt: A team runs everything with Terraform today. Which move costs the least, and why?
hint: What did this lesson measure?

choices.text: To the CDK, since it can import the Terraform state
choices.why: The CDK has no use for a Terraform state; every resource would be imported into a stack.

choices.text: To Pulumi, since its providers are bridged from Terraform's
choices.why: Similar arguments help, but the program is a rewrite and every resource an import.

choices.text: To OpenTofu, which reads the very same files and state
choices.why: Yes: the same files and the same state, as long as nothing only Terraform knows is used.

choices.text: To CloudFormation, since AWS keeps the state for you
choices.why: Keeping the state is easier afterwards; getting there is a rewrite plus imports.

prompt: A colleague's machine runs `tofu` with no mirror and full internet access, on this lesson's configuration, whose `versions.tf` names the provider by its full address. Where does `tofu init` look for the provider?
hint: A full address leaves nothing to fill in.

choices.text: `registry.opentofu.org`, its default
choices.why: A default only applies when the hostname is left out.

choices.text: In that machine's mirror directory
choices.why: That machine has no mirror configured.

choices.text: `registry.terraform.io`, as written
choices.why: Right: the address names that registry, so that is where it asks.

choices.text: Nowhere: OpenTofu refuses hostnames other than its own
choices.why: In this lesson it accepted that exact address.

prompt: Ana wants a reviewer to see, before anything changes, what a CDK edit will do to a deployed stack. Which step gives them that?
hint: Each tool has a name for its plan.

choices.text: Reading `app.js` in the pull request
choices.why: One line reached six resources; the program does not show that.

choices.text: `cdk diff`, against the deployed template
choices.why: Yes: it compares the new template with the deployed one, and on a real account asks for a change set too.

choices.text: `cdk synth`, then `cdk deploy`
choices.why: Deploying is the change itself, not a review of it.

choices.text: `cdk bootstrap`, which compares stacks
choices.why: Bootstrap prepares an account and region; it compares nothing.

prompt: Match each tool to its review step, the thing you read before the change happens.
hint: Each tool has its own word for a plan.

prompt: Ana encrypts an OpenTofu state as in lesson 12 and later decides to go back to Terraform. What has to happen first?
hint: Terraform could not read that file.

choices.text: Nothing: the state format is the same `version` 4
choices.why: Only while nothing like encryption is used; Terraform read the encrypted file as having no version.

choices.text: Decrypt the state with `tofu` and remove the `encryption` block
choices.why: Right: the configuration belonged to OpenTofu from the moment it used that block.

choices.text: Change the provider source back to `hashicorp/aws`
choices.why: The address is not the obstacle; the encrypted state and the block are.

choices.text: Run `terraform init -upgrade` to install encryption support
choices.why: Terraform has no such support to install.
